episodes.title: Promote Primary & Secondary Domain Controller
episodes.subtitle: DC01 + DC02 / Active Directory
episodes.description: Promote the primary and secondary domain controllers on Windows Server, place them on their own network segment, verify the domain's health, and keep a record of the build.

chapters.label: Plan the build
chapters.title: Give every system a purpose
chapters.description: Understand Active Directory and where the controllers live before choosing names, addresses, and the starting configuration.
chapters.network: DC01 and DC02 are planned on VLAN 10, their own segment. The connections show where identity services will take shape.

chapters.label: Configure DC01
chapters.title: Create the first service point
chapters.description: Create the forest and bring Active Directory Domain Services online on DC01.
chapters.network: DC01 is configured. DC02 remains a planned system until it joins this same domain.

chapters.label: Bring in DC02
chapters.title: Give the domain a second home
chapters.description: Add a second writable controller and understand the availability it provides.
chapters.network: Both controllers serve the domain. The moving connection follows directory replication.

chapters.label: Verify the domain
chapters.title: Check the domain's health
chapters.description: Run DCDiag against each controller, confirm replication in both directions, and check each controller's roles and host firewall.
chapters.network: Select either controller below to follow a health check from the administration viewpoint.

chapters.label: Keep evidence
chapters.title: Leave a build you can explain
chapters.description: Record the configuration, observed results, and follow-up work in your training companion.
chapters.network: The directory now has two service points. Your build record connects choices with evidence.

episodes.outcomeSummary: One domain. Two writable controllers on their own segment. Replication and health checks you can explain and verify.
outcomes: Understand Active Directory
Promote both controllers
Verify and keep evidence

courses.title: Configure DNS
courses.subtitle: Service discovery, zones, records & troubleshooting
courses.description: Learn how DNS lets every domain member find its domain controllers, then build dependable internal name resolution on DC01 and DC02: set each controller's DNS order, configure forward and reverse zones, manage service records, and prove resolution, discovery and failover in the air-gapped training network.
outcomes: Explain how DNS lets members find domain controllers, and plan internal DNS and client settings.
Configure secure AD-integrated zones and maintain records.
Test both resolvers, directory discovery, and client fallback.
Find a DNS fault one layer at a time and record the cause, the fix, and the rollback.

stages.title: Map names to the network
stages.detail: Domain Name System (DNS) turns names into addresses, and for Active Directory it does one more job: it tells every domain member where its domain controllers are. Start from the working directory build, learn what DNS answers and what it doesn't, set each controller's DNS client order, and record which server owns each name and how a client finds it.

stages.title: Configure forward and reverse zones
stages.detail: A zone holds the records for one part of the namespace. Forward lookup answers where a name lives. Reverse lookup answers which name is assigned to an address. AD integration lets the directory replicate zone data between the selected DNS servers.

stages.title: Create and maintain service records
stages.detail: Build a small, intentional record set. A host record identifies a machine; an alias provides a stable service name without making that alias a separate server.

stages.title: Prove resolution and directory discovery
stages.detail: Test each server explicitly before testing client fallback. A successful cached answer does not prove that both DNS servers hold the right records, and a correct DNS answer proves neither a successful sign-in nor access to a protected resource.

stages.title: Find the fault and record the fix
stages.detail: Troubleshoot one layer at a time: client settings, server reachability, authoritative data, replication, and finally the application that uses the name.

courses.outcomeSummary: Names that resolve from either controller. Discovery that survives one being down. Proven, not assumed.

courses.title: Configure domain time
courses.subtitle: The Windows Time hierarchy, the PDC emulator & chrony
courses.description: Give the air-gapped domain one clock it can trust: make SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, the reliable source serving its own clock and check it against an approved reference, keep SBD-DC02, Windows members and Linux servers on the hierarchy, and prove the chain with measured offsets.
outcomes: Explain why Kerberos, logs and certificates need agreeing clocks, and plan the hierarchy, reference, fallback and service path.
Make SBD-DC01, the PDC emulator, the reliable source serving its own clock, with hypervisor time sync off on both controllers.
Keep every Windows member and Linux server on the hierarchy, with nothing from Group Policy or a hypervisor overriding it.
Prove the chain with sources, offsets and events, and fix time faults, a moved PDC emulator role included.

stages.title: Plan the domain's time
stages.detail: Every sign-in, log entry and certificate in this network depends on clocks that agree, and an air-gapped network has no internet time to lean on. Learn why time matters here and how the Windows Time hierarchy carries one clock from SBD-DC01 to every system, then write down the reference, the fallback and the service path you will hold the domain to.

stages.title: Make SBD-DC01 the domain's time source
stages.detail: With no outside time to lean on, the domain's clock is whatever SBD-DC01 says, so make that a deliberate, checked configuration. Take the hypervisor out of both controllers' time, mark SBD-DC01 — the PDC emulator — as the reliable source serving its own clock with no external peer, and run the first check against the approved reference.

stages.title: Bring every system onto the hierarchy
stages.detail: One source is only useful if every other clock follows it and nothing quietly overrides that. Leave SBD-DC02 and the Windows members on the domain hierarchy's defaults, keep Group Policy and hypervisors out of their time, and write the chrony configuration every Linux server in later courses uses to follow both controllers.

stages.title: Prove the time chain
stages.detail: A source you configured is a claim until every link answers to it. Read each system's source and status, measure its offsets and confirm they are small and stable, and keep the events and readings that let an assessor see the time chain for themselves.

stages.title: Find the time fault and record the fix
stages.detail: Time faults rarely look like time: a refused sign-in, a replication error, a certificate that is suddenly not yet valid. Measure the offset first, find where the hierarchy broke — a member off its source, a moved PDC emulator role, a restored or reverted VM — then fix the cause, resync safely and record what happened.

courses.outcomeSummary: One declared, checked clock on SBD-DC01. Every system following it. Offsets measured, not assumed.

courses.title: Measure against the STIG
courses.subtitle: DISA STIGs, SCAP scans & STIG Viewer checklists
courses.description: Stage the DISA SCAP tools and content across the air gap, scan SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 against the Windows Server STIG with SCC, answer the manual checks in STIG Viewer checklists, and hand course 1.5 a classified findings record traced to NIST SP 800-53 controls.
outcomes: Explain STIGs, SRGs, SCAP benchmarks, severity categories and CCIs, and what a scan can and cannot prove.
Stage SCC, STIG Viewer, the STIGs and the DISA GPO package across the air gap with hashes verified on both sides.
Capture a hashed SCAP baseline of both controllers and complete STIG Viewer checklists with observed evidence.
Classify every open finding and hand course 1.5 a versioned findings record traced to NIST controls.

stages.title: Understand STIGs, SCAP and checklists
stages.detail: A Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) is DISA's configuration standard for one product, and every scan and checklist in this course measures against one. Learn how a rule is identified, rated and traced to NIST SP 800-53, which rules a scanner can read and which a person must answer, then record which STIGs apply to each controller.

stages.title: Stage the DISA content across the air gap
stages.detail: Everything this course and the next one use is downloaded DISA content: the SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC), STIG Viewer, the SCAP benchmarks, the STIGs and the Group Policy object (GPO) package. It crosses the boundary the way everything does here — reviewed, hashed, and carried on approved removable media.

stages.title: Capture the pre-hardening baseline
stages.detail: Measure before you change. A scan of the freshly built controllers shows the honest starting point, teaches what the operating system already secures by default, and becomes the before picture every later scan is compared against.

stages.title: Build the checklists and answer the manual checks
stages.detail: A scan answers only what it can read. In STIG Viewer on SBD-DC01, build a checklist for each controller and one for the directory, let the SCC results fill the automated rules, and answer every remaining rule with what you observed.

stages.title: Write the findings record for hardening
stages.detail: A checklist full of statuses is not yet a decision. Turn the open items from all three checklists into one findings record — counted by severity, classified, owned, and traced from rule to CCI to NIST control — that course 1.5 can harden against and prove.

courses.outcomeSummary: Both controllers measured against the STIG. Every open item counted, classified, and handed to course 1.5.

courses.title: Harden with Group Policy
courses.subtitle: OU design, Group Policy processing & DISA GPOs proven by rescan
courses.description: Build the organizational units the hardening hangs on, learn exactly how Group Policy decides what applies, import the DISA STIG Group Policy objects course 1.4 staged and link them to SBD-DC01 and SBD-DC02 by OU, and prove the change with a rescan matched to course 1.4's baseline, updated checklists and an owned exception record.
outcomes: Design OUs for delegation and policy targeting, and redirect the default containers.
Predict which GPO wins from processing order, link order, inheritance, filtering and loopback, and confirm it with gpresult.
Import the DISA GPO package through the central store and link it by OU, with account policies at the domain root.
Prove the hardening with a rescan matched to course 1.4's baseline, updated checklists and an owned exception record.

stages.title: Design and build the OU structure
stages.detail: Organizational units exist for delegation and Group Policy targeting, not to mirror an org chart. Build the structure the hardening policies will hang on before importing any of them.

stages.title: Learn how Group Policy applies
stages.detail: Before the DISA settings arrive, learn how a computer decides which Group Policy objects (GPOs) apply and which setting wins. Map the order, build the central store the import will use, and record what both controllers apply today.

stages.title: Import and link the DISA GPOs
stages.detail: Group Policy is how the STIG becomes configuration. Import the package course 1.4 staged, link each policy where its systems live so the findings marked fix by GPO can close, and keep the lab's deliberate deviations written down rather than silently skipped.

stages.title: Rescan, reconcile, and record
stages.detail: The second scan is the verdict. Rescan with exactly the versions course 1.4 used, compare each controller with its own baseline, update copies of the course 1.4 checklists, and give every remaining open item an answer.

stages.title: Set the rescan cadence and exception record
stages.detail: Hardening is a state you maintain, not a step you finish. Close the course with an owned exception record and a recorded policy state — reports and links, while course 1.19 backs the GPOs up — and decide who rescans, when, and which event forces an early look.

courses.outcomeSummary: OUs built for delegation, DISA policies applied where they belong, and a rescan that proves what changed.

stages.title: Design the two-tier trust hierarchy
stages.detail: The root establishes trust. The subordinate, also called the issuing CA in this design, handles approved end-entity certificates. Keeping these roles separate protects the root from daily network exposure.

stages.title: Configure the offline Root CA
stages.detail: Treat root installation as a controlled event. Its private key is the highest-value secret in the hierarchy, and its configuration shapes the subordinate certificate it will sign.

stages.title: Create the issuing CA request
stages.detail: Prepare the online issuing server, but keep issuance paused until its CA certificate has been signed and installed. The request carries the public key; the private key stays protected on the issuing system or its approved key provider.

stages.title: Sign through the offline ceremony
stages.detail: A signing ceremony connects an approved request to an approved CA identity. A matching filename alone is not proof that the root should trust the request.

stages.title: Activate the issuing CA and distribute trust
stages.detail: A signed certificate is not yet a working CA. Install it, start Certificate Services, set the AIA and CDP locations every issued certificate will carry, and distribute the approved root through managed domain policy.

stages.title: Build the pki.sbd.test publication site
stages.detail: Every certificate the issuing CA has signed carries the pki.sbd.test URLs inside it. This lesson gives those URLs a real home: a small web site on SBD-PKI-MGMT01 serving certificates and revocation lists to the whole network.

stages.title: Publish the trust data at its advertised URLs
stages.detail: A publication site is only correct when the filenames it serves match the URLs the certificates already carry. Copy the current certificates and CRLs into place, wire the issuing CA to keep them fresh, and prove retrieval from a client that has never cached anything.

stages.title: Separate template administration
stages.detail: Certificate templates are directory objects, and whoever edits them decides what the PKI will sign. Give that power its own seat — SBD-PKI-MGMT01 — with named administrators, instead of leaving it wherever a CA console happens to be open.

stages.title: Publish the first working templates
stages.detail: The default template set is a menu, not a deployment. Duplicate the three templates this network actually needs — domain controller, computer and server authentication — set their cryptography deliberately, and publish only those.

stages.title: Validate enrollment, revocation, and renewal
stages.detail: Finish the way relying systems see it: both domain controllers and a pilot machine enroll on their own, validate against the live publication site, and reject a certificate you revoke — then the closing scans record what this course changed and close course 1.4's domain controller certificate finding.

courses.title: Configure the two-tier PKI
courses.subtitle: Offline root, issuing CA, pki.sbd.test publication & templates
courses.description: Build a complete two-tier public key infrastructure: an offline standalone Root CA and an enterprise issuing CA, signed through a controlled ceremony, with trust data served from pki.sbd.test at the exact embedded URLs, template administration on its own seat, certificates for both domain controllers, and enrollment and revocation proven end to end.
outcomes: Design the CA hierarchy and its publication dependencies.
Configure the offline root and sign an issuing CA request through controlled media transfer.
Publish certificates and CRLs at the exact URLs issued certificates carry, from pki.sbd.test.
Move template administration to a delegated seat, give both domain controllers their certificates, and prove autoenrollment and revocation end to end.
courses.outcomeSummary: An offline root, a working issuing CA, and trust data served at exactly the URLs every certificate carries.

courses.title: Run DHCP on SBD-DHCP01
courses.subtitle: Workstation leases, secure name registration & an audited lease trail
courses.description: Design and build the workstation VLAN's addressing service on SBD-DHCP01: a full-subnet scope with exclusions and the three options clients trust, directory authorization, the core's relay verified rather than built, client names registered under one dedicated low-privilege account with name protection, a lease history kept beyond Windows' weekly overwrite, the restore note course 1.19's backup relies on, and a proof that a name takeover fails.
outcomes: Design the VLAN 80 scope, its exclusions, lease length, and options, and confirm the core's relay under F04.
Build and authorize SBD-DHCP01 on a member server run by its own server-administration accounts.
Register client names under one dedicated account with name protection, never through DnsUpdateProxy.
Keep the lease history, write the restore note for course 1.19's backup, and prove the service, including a refused name takeover.

stages.title: Design the addressing service
stages.detail: DHCP decides the first things every workstation believes: its address, its gateway, and which servers answer its names. Design that service before building it — one scope for VLAN 80, the options clients will trust, and the identities that authorize, run, and register for it — and confirm the core already relays VLAN 80's requests.

stages.title: Build SBD-DHCP01 and its scope
stages.detail: Addressing is the first service fifty machines will ask for. Build the DHCP server on a member server run by its own administration accounts, authorize it in the directory — the check that keeps unauthorized Windows DHCP servers from serving — and create the VLAN 80 scope, then pull a first lease through the core's relay.

stages.title: Register client names securely
stages.detail: Course 1.2's zone accepts only secure updates, so the real question is who writes VLAN 80's records. Give that job to one dedicated, unprivileged account, turn on name protection so no device can take over another's name, and keep the DnsUpdateProxy group empty — it strips the protection off every record its members create.

stages.title: Audit leases and write the restore note
stages.detail: A router's deny log names addresses, not machines; the DHCP audit log is how you turn an address at a moment in time into a workstation. Keep that log longer than the week Windows keeps it, review who holds leases, know what an unauthorized DHCP server can and can't do here, and write the restore note that course 1.19's backup of the server relies on.

stages.title: Prove the service and hand off
stages.detail: Prove DHCP the way clients will meet it: the test client gets the right lease and its name registers securely, a device that tries to take that name is refused, and the evidence lands in the logs. Then take SBD-DHCP01's first SCAP baseline and hand the server to course 1.8, which moves its administration to the Tier 1 seat.

courses.outcomeSummary: Addresses handed out on purpose, with names no device can take over.

courses.title: Tiered administration
courses.subtitle: Admin seats, the tier rules & where privilege may sign in
courses.description: Build the administration plane before the fleet: three administration seats on two machines in VLAN 60 (the endpoint seat runs as a virtual machine on the server seat), directory-enforced tier restrictions proven by both successful in-tier sessions and logged out-of-tier denials, and the move of earlier console work — SBD-DHCP01's administration and the assessment tools — onto the seats.
outcomes: Stand up single-purpose administration seats for each tier in the Admin OU, with the endpoint seat a virtual machine on the server seat.
Enforce and prove per-tier sign-in restrictions with captured denial evidence.
Move SBD-DHCP01's administration and the assessment tools onto the seats, each tier on its own.

stages.title: Design the tiers and the admin seats
stages.detail: Tiering is one sentence with teeth: credentials that control a tier never touch a less-trusted one. Write that policy against the OU structure and give each tier its seat and its group — all before any host is built.

stages.title: Build the administration systems
stages.detail: Privileged work gets dedicated, hardened seats: a Tier 0 jump host that runs no virtual machines, and a server-administration seat that also runs the endpoint seat as a virtual machine. Each seat sits in the Admin OU, does nothing but administer, and is maintained by its own group.

stages.title: Restrict where privilege can sign in
stages.detail: The tier rule becomes real when the directory refuses the wrong sign-in. Give Tier 0 servers their own OU first, deny privileged logons on lower tiers by policy, protect the highest accounts, and make the refusal something you can show in a log.

stages.title: Prove the tiers end to end
stages.detail: Run the matrix: every tier's administration works from its seat, every cross-tier attempt fails with an event, and course 1.7's addressing service still behaves exactly as registered.

stages.title: Move the scan tools, rescan, and hand off
stages.detail: Three new seats joined, SBD-DHCP01 changed hands, and the directory's logon policy changed — the cadence fires again. Move the assessment tools off the domain controllers onto the seats, baseline the three seats, rescan what changed, and hand the next course a network administered only from somewhere safe.

courses.outcomeSummary: Privileged sessions that only ever start from the right seat.

courses.title: Build the Linux repository on SBD-REPO01
courses.subtitle: Mirrored, signature-verified package snapshots for the Linux servers
courses.description: Build the one approved source of operating-system packages before any Linux server exists: verify the vendor's signing keys, build and harden SBD-REPO01 on VLAN 70 as a minimal web server, mirror and publish dated snapshots carried across the air gap and checked by hash and signature, write the client configuration every Linux server will use, and prove promotion, rollback and the first STIG baseline with the SCC for Linux set every Linux server is scanned with.
outcomes: Design the Linux package source: one Red Hat Enterprise Linux–family distribution, the repositories mirrored, verified upstream keys, and the register rows.
Build SBD-REPO01 as a hardened, minimal web server administered only from the Tier 1 seat.
Mirror, verify and publish dated snapshots, with promotion and rollback on record.
Hand later courses a tested client configuration that trusts only SBD-REPO01 and the verified keys.

stages.title: Design the repository and its trust
stages.detail: Before anything is mirrored, decide what SBD-REPO01 is for: the one approved source of operating-system packages for the domain-joined Linux servers, fed by dated snapshots whose upstream signing keys you verified first. Then place it on VLAN 70 and write its rows into the register.

stages.title: Build and harden SBD-REPO01
stages.detail: Build SBD-REPO01 as a minimal Linux server that does one job: answer package requests on TCP 80 and accept administration on SSH from one seat. Every other service, listener and account is left out.

stages.title: Mirror, verify, and publish a snapshot
stages.detail: The repository's content crosses the boundary like everything else: mirrored on the connected side, hashed, carried across, and checked twice on arrival, once against the hash manifest and once against the vendor's signatures. Only then is it published as a dated snapshot and entered in the catalog.

stages.title: Configure the Linux clients
stages.detail: Write the one client configuration every Linux server will use: a single source definition pointing at SBD-REPO01, the verified signing keys, and no other source. No consumer exists yet, so prove it on SBD-REPO01's own package manager and hand the files to courses 1.12 and 1.18.

stages.title: Keep it current and prove it
stages.detail: A repository is only as good as its last snapshot. Set the cadence that keeps it current, rehearse promoting a new snapshot and rolling back, stage SCC for Linux for every Linux server and take SBD-REPO01's first SCAP baseline with it, and close the course with a record an assessor can check.

courses.outcomeSummary: One verified source of Linux packages, ready before the first Linux server arrives.

courses.title: Collect the record on SBD-SYSLOG01
courses.subtitle: Design the logging pipeline and build its collector
courses.description: The first of three logging courses: design the whole collect → protect → analyze pipeline, then build its first stage — advanced audit policy on the DCs and admin hosts, source-initiated Windows Event Forwarding from every existing Windows system and a syslog intake on SBD-SYSLOG01, health checks with a named owner, and proof that real events arrive with the right names and times.
outcomes: Design all three logging stages: retention, readers, streams, and register rows.
Write the designed audit events on the DCs and admin hosts through GPO.
Forward every existing Windows system's events by source-initiated subscription and take syslog from the router and SBD-REPO01.
Keep the collector healthy and prove collection with events you cause.

stages.title: Design collect, protect, analyze
stages.detail: Three systems, three distinct jobs: SBD-SYSLOG01 gathers, SBD-AUDIT01 preserves, SBD-SPLUNK01 answers questions. This course builds the first; courses 1.11 and 1.12 build the other two — so decide now, for all three, what is collected, how long it lives, who may touch it, and where each stream is picked up.

stages.title: Turn on the right auditing
stages.detail: Forwarding garbage faster is not monitoring. Set the advanced audit policy so the events that tell the network's story — sign-ins, account changes, directory changes, policy changes — actually get written, at or above the STIG values course 1.4 measured.

stages.title: Build the collector
stages.detail: SBD-SYSLOG01 becomes the funnel: Windows Event Forwarding brings in the events of every Windows system that exists by source-initiated subscription, and a syslog receiver takes the core router's denies and, from lesson 5, the Linux servers over TLS — one host where the network's record first lands.

stages.title: Keep the collector trustworthy
stages.detail: A collector that silently stops is worse than none, because everyone assumes it works. Watch the subscription's runtime status, the sources that went quiet, the log's size and overwrite behavior, the disk, and the syslog intake — and decide who is told when collection fails.

stages.title: Prove collection and hand off
stages.detail: Prove the collector with events you cause on purpose: a failed sign-in, a denied probe, and a test message from SBD-REPO01, the first Linux source. Each must land with the right source name and time — then the cadence scans close the course.

courses.outcomeSummary: Every important event written, collected in one place, and proven to arrive with its true source and time.

courses.title: Protect the record on SBD-AUDIT01
courses.subtitle: Keep the audit record intact, even from its administrators
courses.description: The second of three logging courses: build SBD-AUDIT01 as the protected home for the collector's record — daily archives over encrypted SMB from a write-only managed account, SHA-256 hashes cataloged on arrival and verified every day, access auditing that leaves the box, retention that runs only as an approved and logged process, and proof that an administrator's delete is refused and a tampered copy is caught.
outcomes: Design and build the repository: retention, capacity, one write path, and the custodian's separate administration.
Archive the collector's streams daily over encrypted SMB from a write-only gMSA, with every archive hashed and cataloged.
Verify the catalog daily, audit access to the repository, and run retention as an approved, logged process.
Prove an administrator's delete is refused and logged, a tampered copy is caught, and an old archive can still be read.

stages.title: Design the repository and build SBD-AUDIT01
stages.detail: The repository has one job: keep the collector's record intact for its whole retention period, even from its own administrators. Size it, fix the one way in, name every identity and what it may do, and build SBD-AUDIT01 where the model puts it — before a single archive arrives.

stages.title: Archive, hash, and protect the record
stages.detail: The repository is where the record outlives mistakes and attackers alike: daily archives from the collector over an encrypted share, hashed before they leave and again on arrival, readable by few, and deletable by process only.

stages.title: Verify the catalog and watch the repository
stages.detail: A catalog nobody checks is a list of hopes. Re-hash every archive on a schedule, treat a mismatch as a finding, audit who reads or tries to change the repository, and keep the readers as few as the day they were approved.

stages.title: Run retention and prove retrieval
stages.detail: Retention cuts both ways: records must last the full period, and they must go when it ends — by a process with a log, never by a person's right-click. Run retention the way the design says, then prove the other half: an archive from the past can be found, verified, and read.

stages.title: Prove the record survives and hand off
stages.detail: Test the protection the way an attacker or a careless administrator would: try to delete an archive and tamper with a copy, and check that each attempt is refused or caught, and recorded. Then take SBD-AUDIT01's first baseline and hand the record to analysis.

courses.outcomeSummary: A record that arrives by one encrypted path, proves its own integrity every day, and outlives even its administrators.

courses.title: Analyze the record in SBD-SPLUNK01
courses.subtitle: Search a working copy, own the alerts, prove the chain
courses.description: The last of three logging courses: build SBD-SPLUNK01 as a domain-joined Linux server patched only from SBD-REPO01, install Splunk Enterprise from hashed media, forward the collector's two streams over TLS, build the searches that answer this network's first questions, turn them and the pipeline's own failures into alerts someone owns, and trace one event from its source through the collector and the repository to the analyst's screen.
outcomes: Plan analysis — indexes, a retention period set for your environment, roles, and console paths — and build SBD-SPLUNK01 on domain time, patched only from SBD-REPO01.
Install Splunk Enterprise and forward the collector's two streams over TLS, with counts and times that match the collector.
Build the working searches and turn them, and the pipeline's own failures, into tested alerts with named responders.
Trace one event from its source through the collector and the repository to the analyst's screen.

stages.title: Plan analysis and build SBD-SPLUNK01
stages.detail: Analysis works on a copy, not on the record: SBD-AUDIT01 keeps the evidence, and SBD-SPLUNK01 keeps a searchable working copy, for a period your environment sets, for the people who question them. Decide the indexes, retention, roles, and console paths first, then build the domain-joined Linux host that runs it — patched only from SBD-REPO01 and on domain time from its first boot.

stages.title: Install Splunk and bring in the streams
stages.detail: Install Splunk Enterprise on SBD-SPLUNK01 with the indexes, roles, and TLS receiving port lesson 1 designed, then put a universal forwarder on SBD-SYSLOG01 that reads the collector's two streams and sends them over rule F10. Finish by proving the copy is faithful: Splunk's counts and times must match the collector's.

stages.title: Build the working searches
stages.detail: Analysis earns its place with three working searches: failed privileged sign-ins, the boundary's denies, and the health of time — questions this network can already answer about itself. Build them as an analyst, prove each against an event you caused, and save them for the alerts in lesson 4.

stages.title: Own the alerts
stages.detail: An alert nobody owns is a log entry with extra steps. Turn the working searches and the pipeline's own failure conditions into scheduled alerts, each with a threshold set for your environment, a named responder, and a written first response; test each one by causing it, tune the noise, and set the review cadence AU-6 asks for.

stages.title: Prove the chain and hand off
stages.detail: One deliberate event, followed all the way: a failed privileged sign-in should appear on the source, the collector, the analyst's screen, and the repository's next-morning archive. That trace closes all three logging courses; SBD-SPLUNK01's first baseline and the handoff to the fleet close this one.

courses.outcomeSummary: A working copy that answers real questions, alerts someone owns, and one event traced through all three logging systems.

courses.title: Bring in the fleet
courses.subtitle: 50 Windows endpoints, managed from first boot
courses.description: Join the fifty-workstation fleet to a network that is ready for it: DHCP addressing, OU landing with STIG policy at first boot, Windows LAPS for every local administrator, certificate autoenrollment at scale, 802.1X port admission through NPS on SBD-DHCP01, and a sampled proof with the whole rollout observed by the logging pipeline.
outcomes: Roll fifty endpoints in waves that land hardened, addressed, and registered untouched.
Manage every local administrator with Windows LAPS under the tier model.
Admit only enrolled machines to VLAN 80 ports with 802.1X, proven in monitor mode before enforcement.
Prove the fleet with a defined sample, a failure rule, and pipeline-observed joins.

stages.title: Prepare the fleet rollout
stages.detail: Fifty of anything needs a factory, not fifty craft projects. Settle the image, the names, the join account, and the policy links so every endpoint is born identical — then prove it on paper before proving it on metal.

stages.title: Join the pilot and inspect first boot
stages.detail: Three machines go first, and everything the path has built shows up at once: a DHCP lease through the relay, an OU landing, STIG policy, a DNS record — and the join itself appearing on the analyst's screen.

stages.title: Manage local administrators with Windows LAPS
stages.detail: Fifty identical machines must not share one local administrator password. Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS) gives each endpoint its own rotating secret, stored in the directory, readable by the people the tier model says may have it.

stages.title: Autoenroll the fleet's certificates
stages.detail: Course 1.6 proved autoenrollment on both domain controllers and its pilot, SBD-PKI-MGMT01; this lesson turns it loose. Widen the template permission to a fleet computer group, let the autoenrollment GPO already linked at the domain root do the enrolling, and verify a machine certificate chains and checks revocation across the boundary.

stages.title: Admit only enrolled devices with 802.1X
stages.detail: Until now, anything plugged into a VLAN 80 port got an address. With 802.1X, the switch asks each machine to prove who it is with the certificate it enrolled. This lesson turns that check on in monitor mode — every result is logged, nothing is blocked yet — because 47 PCs have no certificate until they join the domain; lesson 6 enforces it once the whole fleet has enrolled. No new server: the NPS role joins DHCP on SBD-DHCP01.

stages.title: Scale to fifty, enforce 802.1X, and prove by sample
stages.detail: Roll the remaining waves while the ports are still in monitor mode, confirm every PC enrolled its machine certificate and authenticates, then switch the ports to enforcement — and prove the fleet the only honest way at scale: a defined sample, the same checks as the pilot, and a written rule for what a sample failure means.

stages.title: Delta scan the fleet and hand off
stages.detail: The cadence meets its first population: the sampled endpoints get Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) baselines with the Windows client benchmark from SBD-ADMIN-PC01's own SCAP Compliance Checker (SCC) copy, installed in course 1.8, the infrastructure this course changed is rescanned, and the fleet inventory is handed to course 1.15.

courses.outcomeSummary: Fifty endpoints that arrive hardened, certified, and watched from their very first sign-in.

courses.title: Deliver Windows updates from SBD-WSUS01
courses.subtitle: Air-gapped WSUS: offline import, four rings & Group Policy targeting
courses.description: Give every Windows system one road for updates: build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected WSUS server, feed it each month through the export and import path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks, target four rings by Group Policy — pilot, workstations, member servers, then the domain controllers and the rest of Tier 0, installed by hand — and prove the cycle with WSUS reports, spot checks and a first STIG baseline.
outcomes: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected update server with TLS-protected metadata and tier-bound administration.
Carry each month's updates across the air gap by WSUS export and import, hashed on both sides.
Target four update rings with computer groups and Group Policy, with the domain controllers installed last and by hand.
Promote a monthly cycle ring by ring and prove it with compliance reports, spot checks and a first baseline.

stages.title: Design the rings and the Windows update rule
stages.detail: Decide how Windows updates reach the network before any arrive: one road through SBD-WSUS01, four rings that try every update on what the network can lose before what it can't, and a monthly crossing on the media procedure. Then confirm the register already carries the road.

stages.title: Build SBD-WSUS01 as a disconnected server
stages.detail: Build the server the network will take its updates from: a hardened member server on VLAN 20 that never synchronizes, serves metadata over TLS and signed files over HTTP, and is administered only from the two seats the tier model allows. Its scope is decided here, because what crosses each month is whatever that scope holds.

stages.title: Carry updates across the air gap
stages.detail: SBD-WSUS01 never talks to Microsoft. Each month a second WSUS server on the connected side synchronizes the recorded scope and downloads its files; its metadata export and content folder cross on approved media, hashed on both sides, and SBD-WSUS01 imports them — the two-server path Microsoft describes for air-gapped networks.

stages.title: Target the rings with computer groups and Group Policy
stages.detail: Rings become mechanics: a computer group per ring on SBD-WSUS01, plus one for SBD-AUDIT01, client-side targeting so each computer files itself into its ring, and one Group Policy object per ring that names the server, the ring and its install behaviour. The domain controllers get a ring of their own: they download on their own but install only when Tier 0 starts it, and SBD-AUDIT01 waits for its audit custodian the same way.

stages.title: Run the first cycle and prove it
stages.detail: The design meets a real month: approve the imported updates for the pilot, promote them ring by ring on the written soak times, and install the domain controllers by hand. Then prove the result with WSUS's own reports, spot checks on the systems themselves, and the first SCAP baseline of SBD-WSUS01.

courses.outcomeSummary: One road for Windows updates: imported across the air gap, approved ring by ring, and proven.

courses.title: Keep the living inventory on SBD-MGMT01
courses.subtitle: Component inventory, discovery sources & monthly reconciliation
courses.description: Turn course 1.13's fleet snapshot into a living component inventory for the whole network: build SBD-MGMT01 on VLAN 70 as a keeper that reaches into nothing, record every component once with an accountable owner, check the record against what the directory, DHCP, WSUS and SBD-REPO01 already know, and reconcile it every month so drift becomes a finding.
outcomes: Define the inventory's boundary, columns and owners so every component is counted once and accountable.
Build SBD-MGMT01 as a hardened keeper administered only from the Tier 1 seat.
Gather discovery sources through existing administration paths and know what each one proves.
Reconcile recorded and discovered components every month, with a planted test proving detection works.

stages.title: Design the inventory and its keeper
stages.detail: Decide what the component inventory must hold before SBD-MGMT01 exists: every component inside the boundary counted once, and the columns that make each one accountable. Then name the records that can contradict it, and give it a keeper that holds the record without reaching into anything else.

stages.title: Build and harden SBD-MGMT01
stages.detail: Build the inventory's keeper as a small, quiet member server, joined into the Servers OU so the hardening, tier and update policies apply from its first boot. It answers only the Tier 1 seat, and the record sits on its own volume behind permissions that admit administrators alone.

stages.title: Build the living inventory
stages.detail: Course 1.13's fleet inventory was a snapshot of fifty PCs; SBD-MGMT01 makes the whole network's inventory a living record. Every component gets its place, ring, update source, baseline and owner, kept current by the procedures that change it.

stages.title: Feed it from what the network already knows
stages.detail: The inventory says what should exist; the network's own records say what does. Export the directory's computer objects, the DHCP leases, the WSUS computer list, SBD-REPO01's records and the baseline sessions through the sessions administrators already use, and file them on SBD-MGMT01 with hashes, in one shape lesson 5 can compare.

stages.title: Reconcile the inventory and prove it
stages.detail: Compare the record with what the network reports, classify every difference, and prove the comparison catches drift before trusting a clean result. Then take SBD-MGMT01's first SCAP baseline and hand a reconciled inventory — and the monthly habit — to the courses that follow.

courses.outcomeSummary: One record of every component, checked every month against what the network itself reports.

courses.title: Endpoint protection on SBD-EPO01
courses.subtitle: Managed agents, protection policy & DLP from one console
courses.description: Managed endpoint protection and data-loss prevention for every Windows system, run from the single Trellix ePolicy Orchestrator server, SBD-EPO01.

courses.title: Credentialed scanning with SBD-NESSUS01
courses.subtitle: Scoped scan accounts, findings triage & the standing cadence
courses.description: Credentialed vulnerability scanning of the approved target list from the single Nessus server, SBD-NESSUS01, on domain-joined Linux.

courses.title: Stand up the business services
courses.subtitle: Files, database, licensing & web — by documented paths
courses.description: Give the users what the network exists for: SBD-FS01's role-based shares over verified SMB security, SBD-WEB01 serving internal HTTPS from a hardened, domain-joined Linux Apache, SBD-APPS01's licensing service and application API, and SBD-SQL01 running as a managed identity behind exactly one caller — every hop a documented, proven register row.
outcomes: Serve files through role-group permissions with verified SMB signing and encryption.
Run the database as a managed identity, certificate-encrypted, with SBD-APPS01 as its only caller.
Prove the fleet → web → application → database chain with every hop registered and every shortcut denied.

stages.title: Design the service paths and identities
stages.detail: Four services, and before any of them exist: who talks to what over which port, which identity each service runs as, and which groups own access — the register and the directory answer all three before a role installs.

stages.title: Build SBD-FS01 with least-privilege shares
stages.detail: The file server is where access control meets daily life. Build the shares against the role groups, require SMB signing on the server instead of trusting client defaults, and make 'who can read this' a one-lookup question.

stages.title: Build SBD-SQL01 behind its applications
stages.detail: The database runs as a managed identity, encrypts its connections with a real certificate, and answers exactly one caller, SBD-APPS01 — the narrowest audience on the network, by design.

stages.title: Build SBD-APPS01 and SBD-WEB01
stages.detail: The application server and the internal web server complete the dependency chain: fleet to web, web to application, application to database — each hop a register row, the web tier hardened against its Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) guidance, and HTTPS served from the lab's own trust.

stages.title: Reconcile, scan, and hand off
stages.detail: The business services close the way every build course has: the register reconciled against live behavior, the new systems baselined, the inventory updated — and for the first time, the network is functionally complete.

courses.outcomeSummary: Files, licensing, and a three-tier web application, each reachable only by its documented path.

courses.title: Prove you can recover
courses.subtitle: Backups with custody, one rehearsed restore & the closing record
courses.description: Close the Build path by proving the network can come back: every backup in the network defined and scheduled in one place — the directory, the CA under ceremony-grade custody, Group Policy, DHCP, the repository and analysis configuration, the VLAN 40 business services with their permissions, logins and certificates, the log archive, and the living records — in one hashed catalog, a timed restore rehearsal in isolation, and the recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence.
outcomes: Define and schedule every backup in the network — directory, CA, policy, DHCP, repository, analysis configuration, business services, logs, and records — in one verified catalog.
Rehearse a real system state restore in isolation, measured against written objectives.
File the tested-recovery record that completes the Body of Evidence for path 2.

stages.title: Decide what recovery must prove
stages.detail: Recovery starts as a list of promises: which systems and records must be restorable, how old a restored copy may be, how long restoration may take, and the one schedule that says how each is backed up — written as commitments the rest of the course exists to keep.

stages.title: Back up Tier 0: directory, CA, and policy
stages.detail: The Tier 0 rows of the schedule: system state from both controllers, the issuing CA under ceremony-grade protection, and the whole Group Policy estate with its links — plus the quiet feature that handles the most common 'disaster' of all: the Recycle Bin for deleted directory objects.

stages.title: Back up the member servers and records
stages.detail: The rest of the schedule: SBD-DHCP01 and the inventory, SBD-REPO01 and SBD-SPLUNK01, and the business services — SBD-FS01's shares with their permissions, SBD-SQL01's databases with the logins they depend on, SBD-APPS01's and SBD-WEB01's configuration and certificates — then the log archive and the boundary's records, all in one hashed catalog.

stages.title: Carry the copies to the offline cabinet
stages.detail: A backup that sits on the server it protects fails with it. Move a copy of each backup to the offline cabinet by hand, under the same custody rules as any media crossing a boundary, and keep the custody record that proves it.

stages.title: Rehearse a real restore, in isolation
stages.detail: One restore, actually performed: a domain controller's system state brought back on the isolated segment, timed against the objective, verified against the directory — plus the small restore everyone will someday need, from the Recycle Bin.

stages.title: File the recovery record and close the path
stages.detail: The Build path ends the way it worked: owners, schedules, and evidence. The recovery record joins the living documents, the closing SCAP results snapshot the finished network, and the Body of Evidence is ready for the authorization courses to assemble.

courses.outcomeSummary: Backups with custody, one real restore performed in isolation, and the evidence that you can come back.

courses.title: Risk Management Framework
courses.subtitle: Prepare, Categorize, and Select
courses.description: Take the network the Build the Network courses (1.1–1.19) create, the system shown in Inside the Network, through the Prepare, Categorize, and Select steps of the Risk Management Framework (RMF), following NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 with the April 2016 Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) mapped in. Define and register the system, describe and categorize it in a draft System Security Plan, and select its controls with a draft risk assessment and a monitoring strategy, ready for the Body of Evidence in course 2.2.
outcomes: Explain RMF roles and how NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 and the 2016 JSIG organize the steps and their outputs.
Prepare, register, describe, and categorize the Inside the Network practice system.
Select, tailor, and allocate controls with a draft Risk Assessment Report and a monitoring strategy for plan approval.

stages.title: RMF roles, steps, and editions
stages.detail: Explain who performs, assesses, and approves Risk Management Framework (RMF) work, and how NIST and the Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) organize its steps and outputs.
lessons: 01.3 NIST, the JSIG, and their editions

stages.title: Define and register the system
stages.detail: Establish what is being authorized and why: the mission, stakeholders, assets, boundary, information and its life cycle, early risks, and requirements. Then register the system.

stages.title: Describe and categorize the system
stages.detail: Describe the system, justify its confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts in the draft System Security Plan (SSP), and route the categorization for approval. Treat privacy applicability as an explicit decision.

stages.title: Select controls and plan monitoring
stages.detail: Turn the approved categorization into a selected, tailored, and allocated control set, with a draft Risk Assessment Report and a continuous monitoring strategy, ready for plan review and approval.

relatedResources.title: Open the evidence workspace
relatedResources.detail: Six practice artifacts with editable Markdown and CSV starters

courses.outcomeSummary: A registered system, a justified categorization, and a control set with an owner, a reason, a risk picture, and a monitoring strategy, ready for plan approval.

courses.title: Body of Evidence
courses.subtitle: Implement and Assess: document, prove, and test the network
courses.description: Develop the Body of Evidence for the same Inside the Network build through the Risk Management Framework (RMF) Implement and Assess steps, following NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2 with the 2016 Joint Special Access Program Implementation Guide (JSIG) mapped in. Record the controls as implemented, prove them with indexed evidence, prepare and perform an independent assessment, and carry its findings into a Security Assessment Report (SAR) and a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M).
outcomes: Implement the controls, document them as built, and prove them with indexed evidence.
Prepare and perform an independent assessment, and report supported findings in a Security Assessment Report.
Remediate and reassess what can be fixed now, and carry open findings into a risk-ranked POA&M.

stages.title: Implement and document the controls
stages.detail: Implement the selected controls and record them as built in the System Security Plan (SSP) and Security Controls Traceability Matrix (SCTM), in statements an assessor can test.

stages.title: Connect implementation to proof
stages.detail: Collect technical and operational evidence of the as-built system, index it, and correct the SSP and SCTM wherever the evidence and the plan disagree.
lessons: 06.3 The evidence index and the as-built plan

stages.title: Prepare the assessment
stages.detail: Select an independent assessor, hand over current evidence, and get a Security Assessment Plan approved before any testing starts.

stages.title: Perform and report the assessment
stages.detail: Assess the controls as planned, report supported findings in a Security Assessment Report (SAR), and remediate and reassess what can be fixed now.

stages.title: Build the plan of action and milestones
stages.detail: Turn the findings still open into a risk-ranked Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) with accountable owners, resources, dated milestones, and closure criteria.

relatedResources.title: Open the Body of Evidence workspace
relatedResources.detail: Seven practice artifacts with editable Markdown and CSV starters

courses.outcomeSummary: An as-built plan, an approved and independent assessment, and every open finding carried into an accountable action.

courses.title: Authorization to Operate
courses.subtitle: Authorize and Monitor: the package, the decision, and continuous monitoring
courses.description: Take the Body of Evidence for the Inside the Network system through the Authorize and Monitor steps of the Risk Management Framework (RMF) in NIST SP 800-37 Revision 2, with the matching tasks of the Joint Special Access Program (SAP) Implementation Guide (JSIG), 11 April 2016. Assemble the authorization package, brief the risk for the Authorizing Official (AO), record a fictional decision with its terms, conditions, and duration, and keep the authorization current through change, reporting, and disposal before the package capstone.
outcomes: Assemble and submit an authorization package that meets JSIG Task 5-2 and NIST Task R-1.
Brief the risk for the AO’s determination and record a fictional authorization decision with its terms, conditions, and duration.
Keep the authorization current through security impact analysis, ongoing assessment, status reporting, and disposal.

stages.title: Assemble the authorization package
stages.detail: Assemble an authorization package whose plans, assessment results, and open risks agree, and submit it for the authorizing official’s decision.
lessons: 10.1 Package contents in the JSIG and NIST

stages.title: Support the authorization decision
stages.detail: Brief the risk the authorizing official must determine, propose a response to each significant risk, and record what an authorization decision contains.

stages.title: Monitor and maintain authorization
stages.detail: Keep the authorization true as the system changes: analyze each change, assess and report as the strategy requires, support ongoing authorization, and plan disposal.

relatedResources.title: Open the authorization package capstone
relatedResources.detail: Four hour exercise · Assemble, defend, and maintain the practice package

relatedResources.title: Open the package manifest
relatedResources.detail: Organize the evidence and submission records

courses.outcomeSummary: A complete package, an honest risk picture, a decision record with clear conditions, and monitoring that keeps the authorization true.

categories.title: Build the Network
categories.description: Build the complete air-gapped network, one system at a time: the domain controllers, DNS, domain time, STIG measurement and Group Policy hardening, the two-tier PKI, DHCP, tiered administration, the Linux repository, the logging pipeline (collector, protected archive, and analysis), the workstation fleet, Windows updates, the living inventory, business services, and proven recovery. Follow the courses in order, from 1.1 to 1.19.

categories.title: Network Authorization
categories.description: Prepare the network’s Body of Evidence and Authorization to Operate package. Start after the network build, with course 2.1.
